claim: The human brain weighs 2% of the total body mass.
source: The human brain only weighs 2% of the total body mass but is responsible for 20% of resting metabolism (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The human brain is responsible for 20% of resting metabolism.
source: The human brain only weighs 2% of the total body mass but is responsible for 20% of resting metabolism (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Attwell and Laughlin, 2001 and Harris et al., 2012.

claim: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped its sparse coding strategy.
source: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped many aspects of its design, such as its sparse coding strategy (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Lennie, 2003), the biophysics of the mammalian action potential (Alle et al., 2009; Fohlmeister, 2009), and synaptic failure (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levy and Baxter, 1996 and Lennie, 2003.

claim: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped the biophysics of the mammalian action potential.
source: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped many aspects of its design, such as its sparse coding strategy (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Lennie, 2003), the biophysics of the mammalian action potential (Alle et al., 2009; Fohlmeister, 2009), and synaptic failure (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alle et al., 2009 and Fohlmeister, 2009.

claim: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped synaptic failure.
source: The brain's energy need is believed to have shaped many aspects of its design, such as its sparse coding strategy (Levy and Baxter, 1996; Lennie, 2003), the biophysics of the mammalian action potential (Alle et al., 2009; Fohlmeister, 2009), and synaptic failure (Levy and Baxter, 2002; Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levy and Baxter, 2002 and Harris et al., 2012.

claim: Experimental evidence suggests that memory formation is an energetically expensive process.
source: But in addition to the costs associated to neural information processing, experimental evidence suggests that memory formation, presumably corresponding to synaptic plasticity, is itself an energetically expensive process as well (Mery and Kawecki, 2005; Plaçais and Preat, 2013; Jaumann et al., 2013; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple experimental studies (Mery and Kawecki, 2005; Plaçais and Preat, 2013; Jaumann et al., 2013; Plaçais et al., 2017).

claim: Fruit flies exposed to associative conditioning died some 20% quicker than control flies after food supply was cut off.
source: To estimate the amount of energy required for plasticity, Mery and Kawecki (2005) subjected fruit flies to associative conditioning spaced out in time, resulting in long-term memory formation. After training, the fly's food supply was cut off. Flies exposed to the conditioning died some 20% quicker than control flies, presumably due to the metabolic cost of plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mery and Kawecki (2005) experimental study.

claim: Fruit flies doubled their sucrose consumption during the formation of aversive long-term memory.
source: Likewise, fruit flies doubled their sucrose consumption during the formation of aversive long-term memory (Plaçais et al., 2017), while forcing starving fruit flies to form such memories reduced lifespan by 30% (Plaçais and Preat, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plaçais et al., 2017.

claim: Forcing starving fruit flies to form long-term memories reduced lifespan by 30%.
source: Likewise, fruit flies doubled their sucrose consumption during the formation of aversive long-term memory (Plaçais et al., 2017), while forcing starving fruit flies to form such memories reduced lifespan by 30% (Plaçais and Preat, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plaçais and Preat, 2013.

claim: Massed learning protocol leads to less permanent forms of learning that don't require protein synthesis.
source: A massed learning protocol, where pairings are presented rapidly after one another, leads to less permanent forms of learning that don't require protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of learning protocols.

claim: Massed learning is energetically less costly than spaced learning.
source: Notably this form of learning is energetically less costly (Mery and Kawecki, 2005; Plaçais and Preat, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mery and Kawecki, 2005 and Plaçais and Preat, 2013.

claim: Beneficial effects of glucose on memory have been reported in rats.
source: In rats (Gold, 1986) and humans (Hall et al., 1989, but see Azari, 1991) beneficial effects of glucose on memory have been reported, although the intricate regulation of energy complicates interpretation of such experiments (Craft et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gold, 1986.

claim: Beneficial effects of glucose on memory have been reported in humans.
source: In rats (Gold, 1986) and humans (Hall et al., 1989, but see Azari, 1991) beneficial effects of glucose on memory have been reported, although the intricate regulation of energy complicates interpretation of such experiments (Craft et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hall et al., 1989, with a contrasting citation to Azari, 1991.

claim: Traditional learning algorithms are metabolically highly inefficient.
source: We demonstrate that traditional learning algorithms are metabolically highly inefficient.
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic caching increases energy efficiency manifold.
source: This algorithm, termed synaptic caching, boosts energy efficiency manifold and can be used with any plasticity rule, including back-propagation.
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic caching can be used with any plasticity rule, including back-propagation.
source: This algorithm, termed synaptic caching, boosts energy efficiency manifold and can be used with any plasticity rule, including back-propagation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through implementation with both perceptron learning and back-propagation in the manuscript.

claim: The perceptron is a single artificial neuron that attempts to binary classify input patterns.
source: A perceptron is a single artificial neuron that attempts to binary classify input patterns.
evidence: This is established knowledge about perceptrons in machine learning.

claim: The perceptron has been used to model plasticity in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
source: It forms the core of many artificial networks and has been used to model plasticity in cerebellar Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about perceptron applications.

claim: The energy required by perceptron learning follows a similar divergence behavior as the number of epochs near critical capacity.
source: The energy required, which is proportional to the number of updates that the weights undergo, follows a similar behavior, Figure 1C.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cerebellar and cortical neurons are operating close to their maximal memory capacity.
source: There is evidence that both cerebellar and cortical neurons are operating close to their maximal memory capacity (Brunel et al., 2004; Brunel, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brunel et al., 2004 and Brunel, 2016.

claim: Classifying 1900 patterns by a neuron with 1000 synapses with traditional perceptron learning requires about 900 times more energy than minimally required.
source: However, the above result demonstrates that for instance classifying 1900 patterns by a neuron with 1000 synapses with the traditional perceptron learning requires about ∼900 times more energy than minimally required.
evidence: This is calculated from the theoretical inefficiency formula and simulation results.

claim: There are forms of plasticity that decay and do not require protein synthesis, such as anesthesia-resistant memory in flies and early-LTP/LTD in mammals.
source: There are forms of plasticity –﻿ anesthesia-resistant memory in flies and early-LTP/LTD in mammals –﻿ that decay and do not require protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about different forms of plasticity.

claim: Transient synaptic changes can be induced using a massed, instead of a spaced, stimulus presentation protocol.
source: Such transient synaptic changes can be induced using a massed, instead of a spaced, stimulus presentation protocol.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plasticity induction protocols.

claim: Transient plasticity is much less energy-demanding than long-term memory in fruit flies.
source: Fruit-fly experiments show that this form of plasticity is much less energy-demanding than long-term memory (Mery and Kawecki, 2005; Plaçais and Preat, 2013; Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple fruit-fly experiments.

claim: Synaptic consolidation, but not transient plasticity, is suppressed under low-energy conditions in mammals.
source: In mammals, there is evidence that synaptic consolidation, but not transient plasticity, is suppressed under low-energy conditions (Potter et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potter et al., 2010.

claim: When transient plasticity does not decay and has no maintenance cost, synaptic caching achieves energy equal to the theoretical minimum.
source: If the transient synaptic component could store information indefinitely at no metabolic cost, consolidation could be postponed until the end of learning and the energy would equal the minimal energy Equation 2.
evidence: This is derived theoretically and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Transient plasticity might correspond to an increased/decreased vesicle release rate.
source: Biophysically, transient plasticity might correspond to an increased/decreased vesicle release rate (Padamsey and Emptage, 2014; Costa et al., 2015) so that it diverges from its optimal value (Levy and Baxter, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Padamsey and Emptage, 2014; Costa et al., 2015; and Levy and Baxter, 2002.

claim: There is an optimal consolidation threshold that balances persistent and transient forms of plasticity.
source: As a result of this trade-off, there is an optimal threshold –﻿ which depends on the decay and the maintenance cost –﻿ that balances persistent and transient forms of plasticity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Synaptic caching can save 80% of the energy in a spiking neural network with biologically plausible learning.
source: The network is able to save 80% of the energy with synaptic caching, Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The implementation of a consolidation threshold resembles the synaptic tagging and capture phenomenon.
source: This resembles the synaptic tagging and capture phenomenon where plasticity induction leads to transient changes and sets a tag; only strong enough stimulation results in proteins being synthesized and being delivered to all tagged synapses, consolidating the changes (Frey and Morris, 1997; Barrett et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frey and Morris, 1997 and Barrett et al., 2009.

claim: All variants of synaptic caching lead to comparable efficiency gains.
source: However, all variants lead to comparable efficiency gains, Figure 4B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Learning without synaptic caching in a back-propagation network is metabolically expensive.
source: Similar to a perceptron, learning without synaptic caching is metabolically expensive in a back-propagation network.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results on MNIST dataset.

claim: Until reaching maximal accuracy, energy rises approximately exponentially with accuracy in back-propagation networks.
source: Until reaching maximal accuracy, energy rises approximately exponentially with accuracy, after which additional energy do not lead to further improvement.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When the learning rate is sufficiently small, the metabolic cost of plasticity is independent of the learning rate.
source: When the learning rate is sufficiently small, the metabolic cost of plasticity is independent of the learning rate.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Traditional learning without synaptic caching expends at least 20 times more energy compared to the theoretical minimum in multilayer networks.
source: Traditional learning without synaptic caching is once again energetically inefficient, expending at least ∼20 times more energy compared to this theoretical minimum whatever the desired accuracy level is, Figure 5B.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There exists an optimal number of neurons to participate in memory formation from an energy perspective.
source: These results show that from an energy perspective there exists an optimal number of neurons to participate in memory formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The optimal number of hidden units depends on the accuracy requirement.
source: The optimal number depends on the accuracy requirement; as expected, higher accuracies require more hidden units and energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Synaptic caching can be applied to any synaptic learning algorithm.
source: We stress that from an algorithmic point of view, synaptic caching can be applied to any synaptic learning algorithm (unsupervised, reinforcement, supervised) and does not have specific requirements.
evidence: This is demonstrated by implementation with multiple learning algorithms in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic consolidation is known to be affected by reward, novelty and punishment.
source: Synaptic consolidation is known to be affected by reward, novelty and punishment (Redondo and Morris, 2011), which is compatible with a metabolic perspective as energy is expended only when the stimulus is worth remembering.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Redondo and Morris, 2011.

claim: Consolidation is competitive, but transient plasticity is less so.
source: In addition, our results for instance explain why consolidation is competitive, but transient plasticity is less so (Sajikumar et al., 2014), namely the formation of long-term memory is precious.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sajikumar et al., 2014 and interpreted through the energy efficiency framework.

claim: Encouraging consolidation increases energy consumption.
source: Consistent with this, there is evidence that encouraging consolidation increases energy consumption (Plaçais et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plaçais et al., 2017.

claim: Sufficient transient plasticity should trigger consolidation, even in the absence of other consolidation triggers.
source: We also predict that the transient weight changes act as an accumulative threshold for consolidation. That is, sufficient transient plasticity should trigger consolidation, even in the absence of other consolidation triggers.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the synaptic caching model.

claim: Combining persistent and transient storage mechanisms is a strategy well known in traditional computer systems.
source: Combining persistent and transient storage mechanisms is a strategy well known in traditional computer systems to provide a faster and often energetically cheaper access to memory.
evidence: This is established knowledge about computer architecture.

claim: The transfer of information is often a bottleneck in computer architectures and consumes considerable power in modern computers.
source: The transfer of information is often a bottleneck in computer architectures and consumes considerable power in modern computers (Kestor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kestor et al., 2013.

claim: In the nervous system, transient and persistent synapses appear to exist next to each other.
source: However, in the nervous system transient and persistent synapses appear to exist next to each other.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about synaptic organization.

claim: Local consolidation in a synapse does not require moving information.
source: Local consolidation in a synapse does not require moving information.
evidence: This is inferred from the biological organization of synapses.

claim: Splitting plasticity into transient and persistent forms might prevent catastrophic forgetting in networks.
source: Splitting plasticity into transient and persistent forms might prevent catastrophic forgetting in networks (Leimer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leimer et al., 2019.

claim: The main benefit of more transient forms of plasticity is to permit the network to explore the weight space to find a desirable weight configuration using less energy.
source: Here, we argue that the main benefit of more transient forms of plasticity is to permit the network to explore the weight space to find a desirable weight configuration using less energy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion derived from the analysis and simulations in the manuscript.

claim: The brain expends significant amounts of energy on spiking, synaptic transmission, and maintaining resting potential.
source: While this work focuses solely on the metabolic cost of synaptic plasticity, the brain also expends significant amounts of energy on spiking, synaptic transmission, and maintaining resting potential.
evidence: This is established knowledge about brain energy consumption.

claim: Learning rules can be designed to reduce costs associated to computation once learning has finished.
source: Learning rules can be designed to reduce costs associated to computation once learning has finished (Sacramento et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sacramento et al., 2015.

claim: The perceptron learning rule is energy inefficient because weight modifications made to correctly classify one pattern are partly undone when learning another pattern.
source: The perceptron learning rule is energy inefficient, because repeatedly, weight modifications made to correctly classify one pattern are partly undone when learning another pattern.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of the perceptron learning algorithm.

claim: As the number of patterns to be classified increases, the cone containing correct weights shrinks and the random walk becomes longer.
source: As the number of patterns to be classified increases, the cone containing correct weights shrinks and the random walk becomes longer (Gardner, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gardner, 1987.

claim: The most energy efficient algorithm would somehow directly set the synaptic weights to their desired final values.
source: The most energy efficient algorithm would somehow directly set the synaptic weights to their desired final values.
evidence: This is a theoretical inference about optimal energy efficiency.

claim: When the consolidation threshold is low, consolidation occurs often and the energy approaches the one without synaptic caching.
source: When the threshold is low, consolidation occurs often and the energy approaches the one without synaptic caching.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When the consolidation threshold is high, the expensive consolidation process occurs rarely, but the maintenance cost of transient plasticity is high.
source: When on the other hand the consolidation threshold is high, the expensive consolidation process occurs rarely, but the maintenance cost of transient plasticity is high; moreover, the decay will lead to forgetting of unconsolidated memories, slowing down learning and increasing the energy cost.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When decay is rapid, it is best to consolidate frequently as otherwise information is lost.
source: In the other limit, when the decay is rapid (right-most region), it is best to consolidate frequently as otherwise information is lost.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When maintenance cost is high, it is of primary importance to keep learning time short.
source: When maintenance cost is high, it is of primary importance to keep learning time short, and in fact the learning time can be lower than in a perceptron without decay, Figure 3, bottom, light curves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: When maintenance cost is low, the optimal solution is to set the consolidation threshold high so as to minimize the number of consolidation events, even if this means a longer learning time.
source: When on the other hand maintenance cost is low, the optimal solution is to set the consolidation threshold high so as to minimize the number of consolidation events, even if this means a longer learning time, Figure 3, bottom, dark curves.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: For intermediate decay rates, the consolidation threshold trades off between learning time and energy efficiency.
source: For intermediate decay rates, the consolidation threshold trades off between learning time and energy efficiency, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By setting the consolidation threshold the perceptron can learn either rapidly or efficiently.
source: That is, by setting the consolidation threshold the perceptron can learn either rapidly or efficiently.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When the transient component decays, synaptic caching can not only reduce metabolic cost but can also reduce learning time.
source: In summary, when the transient component decays the learning dynamics is altered, and synaptic caching can not only reduce metabolic cost but can also reduce learning time.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Efficiency gains from synaptic caching do not rely on exact implementation.
source: Hence, efficiency gains from synaptic caching do not rely on exact implementation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by implementation in both abstract and biophysical models.

claim: Consolidation of one synapse leads to consolidation of another synapse that would otherwise decay back to baseline in synaptic tagging and capture experiments.
source: Only cases 2 and 3 are consistent with synaptic tagging and capture experiments, where consolidation of one synapse also leads to consolidation of another synapse that would otherwise decay back to baseline (Frey and Morris, 1997; Sajikumar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frey and Morris, 1997 and Sajikumar et al., 2005.

claim: At larger learning rates, learning no longer converges and energy goes up steeply without an increase in accuracy.
source: At larger learning rates, learning no longer converges and energy goes up steeply without an increase in accuracy, Figure 5A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Lowering the learning rate does not save energy in back-propagation networks (except at very large rates).
source: With the exception of these very large rates, these results show that lowering the learning rate does not save energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The network fails to reach the desired accuracy if the number of hidden units is too small.
source: The network fails to reach the desired accuracy if the number of hidden units is too small, Figure 5C.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When the network size is barely above the minimum requirement, the network has to compensate the lack of hidden units with longer training time and hence a larger energy expenditure.
source: When the network size is barely above the minimum requirement, the network has to compensate the lack of hidden units with longer training time and hence a larger energy expenditure.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Very large networks require more energy.
source: However, very large networks also require more energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Higher accuracies require more hidden units and energy.
source: The optimal number depends on the accuracy requirement; as expected, higher accuracies require more hidden units and energy.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Energy requirements rise steeply as memory load or designated accuracy level increase.
source: We have shown that energy requirements rise steeply as memory load or designated accuracy level increase.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation data shown in Figures 1C and 5A.

claim: There are trade-offs between energy consumption, and network capacity and performance.
source: This indicates trade-offs between energy consumption, and network capacity and performance.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of energy requirements at different capacity and accuracy levels.

claim: Further energy savings might be possible by adjusting the consolidation threshold as learning progresses.
source: Further savings might be possible by adjusting the consolidation threshold as learning progresses and by being pathway-specific (Leibold and Monsalve-Mercado, 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about potential improvements, with citation to Leibold and Monsalve-Mercado, 2016.

claim: Synaptic caching gives a novel interpretation of synaptic tagging and capture findings.
source: Our results thus give a novel interpretation of those findings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of existing experimental findings through the synaptic caching framework.

claim: The formation of long-term memory is precious from an energy perspective.
source: In addition, our results for instance explain why consolidation is competitive, but transient plasticity is less so (Sajikumar et al., 2014), namely the formation of long-term memory is precious.
evidence: This is an interpretation derived from the energy efficiency framework.

claim: Biology appears to have found a more efficient way to store information than traditional computer systems.
source: Using this setup, biology appears to have found a more efficient way to store information.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing biological synaptic organization to computer cache systems.

claim: The main benefit of more transient forms of plasticity is to permit the network to explore the weight space using less energy.
source: Here, we argue that the main benefit of more transient forms of plasticity is to permit the network to explore the weight space to find a desirable weight configuration using less energy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion derived from the analysis and simulations in the manuscript.

claim: The multilayer networks use one hidden layer with logistic units and one-hot encoding at the output.
source: For the multilayer networks trained on MNIST, we use networks with one hidden layer, logistic units, and one-hot encoding at the output.
evidence: This describes the neural network architecture used in the study.

claim: Weights in the multilayer network are updated according to the mean squared error back-propagation rule without regularization.
source: Weights are updated according to the mean squared error back-propagation rule without regularization.
evidence: This describes the learning algorithm used in the study.

claim: The variance in the weights during perceptron learning is about 20% smaller than a random walk.
source: Simulations show that the variance in the weights is actually about 20% smaller than a random walk, likely reflecting correlations in the learning process not captured in the random walk approximation.
evidence: This is observed from simulation data.

claim: The slight deviation in the inefficiency between theory and simulation is explained by correlations in the learning process not captured in the random walk approximation.
source: This explains most of the slight deviation in the ineffeciency between theory and simulation, Figure 1D.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing theoretical predictions to simulation results.

claim: Equations 6 and 7 give a good prediction of the simulation when provided with the time-varying update probability from the simulation.
source: However, Equations 6 and 7 give a good prediction of the simulation when provided with the time-varying update probability from the simulation, Figure 6.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing theoretical predictions to simulation data in Figure 6.
